paraphrase: Opening salutation: Oṃ, obeisance to the Primal One, set forth by the Vedas; victory to the one known by itself, whose form is the Self.

original.text: ॐ नमोजी आद्या । वेदप्रतिपाद्या । जय जय स्वसंवेद्या । आत्मरूपा ॥
original.edition: recalled from memory; to be checked against a printed edition

paraphrase: After the opening, Jñāneśvar pictures Gaṇeśa as the Word itself — the Vedas and śāstras as his limbs — salutes Śāradā, and bows to his guru Nivṛtti, by whose grace alone he is able to speak.

Expanding the marks of the devotee dear to Kṛṣṇa (BhG 12.13–20), Jñāneśvar has the Lord say he carries such a devotee on his head and longs to see him: one without hatred, friendly and compassionate to all, the same in honour and dishonour, content, whose mind is given to him.

Jñāneśvar dwells at length on humility, non-violence, patience, straightforwardness and the other qualities the Gītā calls 'knowledge' (BhG 13.7–11), insisting that knowledge is recognised by these qualities in conduct, not by learning.

On the field and its knower (BhG 13.1–6), Jñāneśvar expands the list of what makes up the field — the elements, ego, intellect, the unmanifest, the senses and mind, their objects, desire, aversion, pleasure, pain and the rest — and teaches that the knower of every field is the Lord.

On the three guṇas (BhG 14), Jñāneśvar describes how sattva binds through attachment to happiness and knowledge, rajas through attachment to action, tamas through delusion and sloth, and teaches that one who serves the Lord with undeviating devotion passes beyond them (BhG 14.26).

The closing prayer (Pasāydān): may the Lord who is the Self of the universe be pleased with this sacrifice of words and grant this gift — that the wicked give up their crookedness and delight in good deeds; that friendship grow among all beings; that the darkness of sin depart and the world see by the sun of its own dharma; that every being obtain what it desires; that the assemblies of devotees shower blessings on the earth; and that the three worlds be happy.

original.text: आतां विश्वात्मकें देवें । येणें वाग्यज्ञें तोषावें । तोषोनि मज द्यावें । पसायदान हें ॥
original.edition: recalled from memory; to be checked against a printed edition

notes: Original gives the first ovī only. Verse numbers as in the Sākhare numbering (verify).

paraphrase: At the close of the work Jñāneśvar names his lineage: Śiva taught the secret on the shore of the milk-ocean to Pārvatī; Matsyendra received it (in the fish's belly); he gave it to Gorakṣa, Gorakṣa to Gahinī, and Gahinī to Nivṛtti with the command to share it with all beings, whence it came to Jñāneśvar.
notes: Chapter-level ref: the passage is in the closing ovīs of ch. 18 (c. 18.1750–1760 in common numbering; not checked — the local e-text ends at ch. 16). Details recalled.
speaker: Jñāneśvar

paraphrase: The colophon: the commentary was spoken in Śaka 1212 at Nevāse on the Pravarā, in the reign of the Yādava king Rāmacandra, and written down by Saccidānanda.

On the Gītā's word that one who has become Brahman attains supreme devotion (BhG 18.54–55), Jñāneśvar speaks of a 'fourth' devotion beyond that of the afflicted, the seeker and the one who wants gain: the knower's devotion, in which God and devotee are one and worship goes on without the sense of two.
notes: Location of the 'fourth devotion' discussion recalled as ch.18; it may also be developed at ch.7 (BhG 7.16–18). Verify.

paraphrase: Jñāneśvar gives his lineage: Śiva (Ādinātha) taught Matsyendranātha, he Gorakṣanātha; Gorakṣa passed the teaching to Gahinīnātha, who gave it to Nivṛttinātha with the charge to relieve the beings of the Kali age; Nivṛtti gave it to Jñāneśvar.
Jñāneśvar promises to tell the teaching in Marathi so skilfully that his words will win a wager even against nectar, choosing syllables full of rasa.
notes: The famous 'mājhā marāṭhācī bolu kautukeṃ' ovī; number approximate.

paraphrase: Then, by the warmth of the seat, the power awakens the kuṇḍalinī: like a young serpent bathed in saffron curled asleep on its bed, the kuṇḍalinī lies asleep, small, in three and a half coils, a she-serpent facing downward.

paraphrase: That kuṇḍalinī is the world-mother, the splendour of the sovereign of consciousness, who shades the sprout of the world-seed; she is the pedestal of the liṅga of the void, the casket of Śiva the supreme self, the open birthplace of the breath.

paraphrase: Commenting on the Gītā's teaching of seated meditation (BhG 6.10–15), Jñāneśvar describes the 'royal road' (pantharāja) of the Nāth yogīs: through posture and the bodily locks the coiled power (kuṇḍalinī), asleep at the base of the body, wakes, rises through the centres consuming the body's elements, and merges into the supreme at the crown; the yogī's body becomes light and radiant and the sense of a separate self dissolves. Summary only (restricted practice).
notes: Existence and gist of the passage certain; ovī range approximate; no steps recorded.

paraphrase: Commenting on the Gītā's teaching that whatever one remembers at death one becomes (BhG 8.5–6), Jñāneśvar urges constant remembrance throughout life, since the mind at the last moment follows its lifelong habit; the one who has remembered the Lord always reaches him.

On the Gītā's promise that women, vaiśyas, śūdras and those of low birth reach the highest by taking refuge in the Lord (BhG 9.32–33), Jñāneśvar says birth and caste count for nothing once one turns to God: as rivers lose their names in the ocean and every kind of wood becomes the same fire, all who come to him become one with him.
